concept.name: Directional exposure
concept.definition: The portion of a portfolio's exposure that profits or loses with the direction of the underlying market — the signed, unhedged sensitivity to price moves, as distinct from offsetting relative-value exposure.
concept.intuition: It answers 'which way does this book need the market to go?': the residual bet left after hedges and offsets are accounted for.
concept.mechanics: Estimated as net exposure or, more refined, beta-adjusted net exposure: signed position values divided by capital, weighting each position by its beta or factor sensitivity so that a high-beta long and a low-beta short are not treated as offsetting one-for-one.
concept.formula: Directional (beta-adjusted) exposure = sum_i ( w_i * beta_i ), where w_i is the signed position weight and beta_i its sensitivity to the reference market; the simple form is net exposure = (longs - shorts) / NAV.
concept.failure_modes: Beta-adjusted versions inherit estimation error in betas, which are unstable and regime-dependent, while simple net-exposure versions miss factor tilts entirely. In dislocations, correlations converge and previously 'nondirectional' books reveal hidden directionality.
concept.misconceptions: Directional exposure is not the same as position count or gross size: a large two-sided book can carry little directional risk, while a modest unhedged position can be entirely directional.
concept.example: Long $1M of a broad index portfolio and short $200k of a large constituent: the short trims the book's directional (net) exposure by $200k against the index.
